items.rss_description: Smarter Approach to Prior Authorization Life & Health ITL Editorial Team Mon, 11/02/2026 - 11:48 Healthcare plans are slashing prior authorization requirements, but smarter technology and mutual accountability may improve care more than blanket reductions. November 16, 2026 Image Prior authorization has been a healthcare sticking point for years. Patients and providers criticize prior authorization (PA) for denying care and coverage. State and federal lawmakers target it, setting standards and policies for how health plans must operate, often without a deep understanding of the complexities of the issue. In response to the public and legislative pressure, many plans are reducing their reliance on PA. UnitedHealthcare announced that it will cut PA requirements by 30% by the end of 2026 , including some outpatient surgeries and diagnostic tests, as well as certain outpatient therapies and chiropractic care. UnitedHealthcare's announcement is just the latest in a series of moves by plans to reduce their reliance on PA. In June 2025, industry organization AHIP committed to six PA reforms across commercial, Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care coverage, including reduced requirements and faster response times. Individual plans also have acted. AHIP reported earlier this year that major insurers had cut 11% of PAs (6.5 million). While reducing PA will certainly eliminate some friction, and please patients and providers, blanket policies are seldom the solution to an issue this complex. Rather, this is an opportunity to take a smarter approach to PA, one that improves care and makes it smarter, fairer, and more efficient for all involved. One that treats PA as a tool for better care rather than a barrier. The cost of poor prior authorization There is no doubt that PA needs to improve. A process that started in the 1960s with the launch of Medicare has become far too cumbersome. Providers say it delays or prevents treatment, adds administrative costs, and overrides their clinical judgment. A 2026 AMA survey found an average of 40 requests per physician per week, taking 13 hours of physician and staff time. Members become frustrated with their plans when approval isn't granted, often without explanation. Plans counter that PA helps ensure appropriate care, block unnecessary or unsafe care, and control costs. Despite all the heat surrounding this issue, there is room – and need – for compromise. Technology has made it possible for PA to be handled far more quickly than in the days of fax machines and phone calls. Both plans and providers also have access to science-backed policies that can better inform their decisions. Rethinking prior authorization It's important to understand that the problems with PA are not the fault of any single party. There needs to be improvement and mutual accountability on both sides in order to improve the process. Plans owe providers and their members transparency in their policies and decision-making, consistent turnaround on claims, and fast, clear decisions. Providers owe plans accurate, evidence-based ordering and complete documentation. This is a precondition for any PA reform to actually work. Without mutual accountability, reducing mandatory PA checks just shifts risk around instead of removing it. It's time to reset our idea of PA from a barrier to care or an indiscriminate way to control spending, to a tool for ensuring patients receive the right care at the right time for the right reason. It should guide and clear the way for timely, effective care. Lab Benefit Management An example of this can be found in lab benefit management (LBM), the governance of lab testing. Clinical testing is the most common medical procedure. Approximately 14 billion lab tests are performed annually, and the results inform 70% of healthcare decisions. However, because individual tests are generally inexpensive, they are not as scrutinized as other procedures. The result is that as much as 30% of testing is unnecessary or redundant, wasting billions of dollars and hindering care. LBM tackles this problem by creating a science-backed set of policies for individual plans. It identifies the tests that offer clinical utility and validity and uses those findings to inform coverage decisions from plans and guide clinicians toward the most effective treatments. However, creating accurate, science-based policies is only the first part of a comprehensive LBM program; the other half is implementing it. Much of the problem with PA is that it is reactive: a clinician submits a request; the plan may reject it for any number of reasons, and it comes back to a frustrated clinician and member, who must try to resolve the issue. Here's a better way: An automated solution trained in plan-specific policies and coverage is integrated into providers' EHRs. It spots inaccurate or missing information in a PA request and flags it for the provider to correct before submission. Once the request is in order and meets the necessary criteria, the solution automatically approves it, removing uncertainty. It also lets the provider know whether the test or treatment is not covered for that patient or if the plan prefers an alternative. A provider can then decide whether to choose another, more appropriate test or proceed with further review by the health plan. In essence, the new process moves the appropriateness review farther upstream to the moment the provider enters an order for a test or procedure, saving time and resources. There are other examples of innovation that link outcomes and PA. The new CMS Cell and Gene Therapy (CGT) Access Model , built around sickle cell disease gene therapies, involves government and drug manufacturers as well as plans and providers. CMS negotiates outcomes-based agreements directly with gene therapy manufacturers on behalf of states. The manufacturers provide guaranteed discounts and pay rebates back if the therapy doesn't deliver the promised clinical benefit. This shifts some of the financial risk from states to manufacturers. This model works because of a safeguard baked into its design: strict upfront criteria to confirm which patients are truly eligible for the therapy. For a one-time, irreversible treatment costing millions of dollars, that kind of appropriateness review isn't a barrier to access — it's what makes access sustainable. The outcome-based rebates manufacturers and states are counting on only hold up if the therapy reaches the patients it's meant for. In that sense, the CGT model and smarter prior authorization share the same logic: verify appropriateness upfront, and both access and affordability take care of themselves. The case for smarter prior authorization The need for a better process to ensure high-quality, appropriate, and affordable care is made more urgent by the explosive growth of precision diagnostics and genetic medicine. These breakthroughs are transforming medicine, offering unprecedented accuracy in diagnostics and new treatments for diseases once thought incurable, but they are expensive and complex. A process like the one described above will remove providers' doubt about which tests are appropriate, streamline the approval process, and enable patients to receive treatment faster. As healthcare organizations and legislators consider PA reform, they should ask themselves if their plans only reduce risk and friction, or whether they truly improve the quality of the care that is being delivered to patients while insisting on accountability from all parties. Varsha Chandramouli

items.title: Insurance Fraud Targets Seniors Online
items.original_title: Insurance Fraud Targets Seniors Online
items.rss_title: Insurance Fraud Targets Seniors Online
items.rss_description: Insurance Fraud Targets Seniors Online Life & Health ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/04/2026 - 13:16 Scammers increasingly impersonate insurers to steal identities and money during open enrollment. November 12, 2026 Image Last year, the Justice Department brought the largest healthcare fraud case in its history, which included charges that criminals stole the identities of more than 1 million Americans to submit $10.6 billion in fraudulent Medicare claims for urinary catheters. While Medicare blocked nearly all of it, private Medicare supplemental insurers paid out about $900 million. Americans lost a record $20.9 billion to internet crime in 2025, up 26% in one year, according to the FBI. Insurance fraud, including healthcare fraud, costs Americans more than $300 billion a year, and health insurance scams pick up during open enrollment, the FTC says. Seniors are the hardest-hit age group, losing $7.7 billion in 2025, up 59% in one year. In fact, Michigan officials warned on Oct. 12 of impostors claiming to be from Medicare to dupe older adults. As co-founder of Spokeo , a people search company, and former co-chair of the W3C Credentials Community Group , I have witnessed firsthand how scammers have grown increasingly sophisticated over the last 20 years. Insurance scams are evolving and costly We are seeing many insurance-related scams in 2026. Fraudsters are buying sponsored search ads with web addresses and logos that look very similar to HealthCare.gov and Medicare.gov . When Americans click on the link, they end up buying a plan that is not real insurance and also fork over their personal information, which can lead to identity theft. Even large health insurers are being duped, as the $900 million loss in the catheter case shows. The Coalition Against Insurance Fraud calls insurance fraud "the crime we all pay for," because it comes back to honest policyholders as higher premiums, which can hurt retention. In a September survey by BrandShield , 30% of U.S. adults said they would stop buying online from brands scammers had impersonated. For an insurer, that is a renewal lost to a scam it never ran. Here are three tips for insurers to help prevent insurance fraud Say what you will never do. Tell customers you will never ask for a one-time code or take payment by gift card, wire or crypto. Put the statement on the ID card, in the app, and on every renewal notice. Explain what numbers to trust and verify. Scammers can spoof caller ID so your company's name appears on a customer's phone. In every fraud alert, encourage customers to use the number on their card and check the identity of incoming callers with a reverse phone search . Report fake ads and websites and warn consumers. Search regularly for impostors using your name and report them to the FBI IC3 , the FTC , and the online platform where they live. Send alerts to customers in real time. Harrison Tang

In a September survey by BrandShield , 30% of U.S. adults said they would stop buying online from brands scammers had impersonated. For an insurer, that is a renewal lost to a scam it never ran. Here are three tips for insurers to help prevent insurance fraud Say what you will never do. Tell customers you will never ask for a one-time code or take payment by gift card, wire or crypto. Put the statement on the ID card, in the app, and on every renewal notice. Explain what numbers to trust and verify. Scammers can spoof caller ID so your company's name appears on a customer's phone. In every fraud alert, encourage customers to use the number on their card and check the identity of incoming callers with a reverse phone search . Report fake ads and websites and warn consumers. Search regularly for impostors using your name and report them to the FBI IC3 , the FTC , and the online platform where they live. Send alerts to customers in real time. Harrison Tang

items.rss_description: November 2026 ITL FOCUS: Pricing & Rating RyanMeyer Mon, 11/02/2026 - 12:00 ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. November 2, 2026 FROM THE EDITOR Pricing is one of the most consequential functions in insurance — and one of the least visible. Claims get the headlines. Underwriting gets the scrutiny. But pricing sits quietly underneath both, shaping profitability across millions of policies through assumptions that can go stale faster than anyone realizes. For most carriers, the mechanics of pricing haven’t kept pace with how quickly the world is changing. A rate change approved today might not be live in the market for weeks or months, trapped behind policy administration release cycles that were never designed for the kind of volatility the industry is now dealing with — social inflation, rising repair costs, tariff pressure, and catastrophe losses that keep defying historical patterns. Kumarappan Sundaram has spent years working through these problems with P&C carriers as a Managing Director at PwC. He brings a technology practitioner’s perspective to a function that often gets treated as a back-office infrastructure problem rather than a strategic capability. He’s measured about where AI fits — distinguishing what is already delivering clear value from what remains genuinely unproven — and direct about the sequencing mistakes carriers make when they try to modernize pricing before the foundation is in place. His practical advice is worth taking seriously: Before reaching for advanced analytics or AI, measure how long it actually takes to get an approved rate change into the market. Most carriers have never done that math. The number, he suggests, tends to be illuminating. Read the full interview to find out why decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is the starting point most carriers skip, how modern pricing platforms are beginning to close the long-standing gap between pricing and underwriting, and where AI can genuinely change the work. Pricing at the Speed of the Market Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet it is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? items.title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.original_title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.rss_title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.rss_description: Why Can't We Fund Prevention? Predict & Prevent ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/04/2026 - 09:29 Industrial organizations excel at financing recovery from asset failures but struggle to justify prevention spending with the same economic rigor. November 5, 2026 Image We've built an extraordinarily sophisticated financial system around industrial failure. We can price it, insure it, reserve capital for it, and finance recovery when it happens, but preventing that same failure often requires an entirely different standard of proof. Insurance is exceptionally good at mobilizing money after something goes wrong. Natural catastrophes caused an estimated $100 billion in economic losses in the first half of 2026. Insurance covered approximately 42%, leaving nearly $60 billion to be absorbed elsewhere. Insurance's ability to fund recovery is indispensable. The shortfall also exposes a contradiction in how risk is funded. Premiums, deductibles, and recovery costs have established places in corporate budgets. A proposal to prevent an asset failure faces a tougher test. Someone must prove the threat is serious, determine what intervention it warrants, and defend spending money on an event that might never happen. Failure has a funding mechanism. Prevention has a business case to make. Insurance can transfer part of a financial loss. It cannot restore missed production, repair damaged customer relationships, or undo the wider consequences of an industrial disruption. The challenge is making prevention as intelligible and investable as recovery. Knowing the risk isn't the same as managing it Industrial organizations rarely lack information. They receive risk-engineering reports, inspection findings, maintenance records and alerts from connected equipment. Yet information doesn't guarantee action. A temperature change, unusual vibration, or a deteriorating component has little meaning in isolation. Its significance depends on the asset's role in the operation. Is there redundancy? What production depends on it? What would a shutdown cost? Could a failure disrupt customers, supply chains or other facilities? These questions turn technical observations into business consequences. Without that translation, recommendations can remain in reports while maintenance teams address more immediate demands and capital committees fund projects with clearer returns. Industry has invested heavily in detecting changing conditions and predicting potential failures. Those capabilities matter. Still, knowing what might fail doesn't tell an organization which emerging risks deserve attention first. A relatively minor condition on a critical asset may represent far greater exposure than a severe condition on equipment with sufficient redundancy. The challenge is understanding what matters most, what the consequences could be, and where intervention will create the greatest value. Prevention needs to compete for capital Consider a manufacturer that identifies deterioration in a critical component on its main production line. Although the component hasn't failed, its condition is changing. The organization must compare the cost of replacing it during a planned shutdown with the lost output, repair time, and disruption that could follow an unplanned failure. The consequences, however, may extend well beyond that production line. A shutdown could affect customer deliveries, contractual commitments, supply-chain continuity and financial performance. What appears to be a maintenance decision may represent a much larger business risk. The appropriate response might be immediate repair, closer monitoring, a change in operating parameters or acceptance of the exposure. Someone must have the authority to make that decision and commit the necessary resources before the opportunity to intervene passes. Now multiply that challenge across hundreds of assets and facilities, each presenting different levels of exposure. The question is no longer simply whether an individual intervention is justified. It's which interventions deserve priority when resources are limited, and the consequences extend across the enterprise. For decades, industry has developed sophisticated ways to measure losses after they occur. We need comparable discipline in understanding the economic value of preventing those losses before they happen. Capital should not only be deployed to absorb loss. It should be possible to direct it intelligently toward preventing loss. The standard for resilience must rise Risk assessments, inspections and engineering recommendations are essential. Completing those processes, however, doesn't necessarily mean an organization has addressed its most consequential exposures. An inspection can establish that a process was followed. A risk assessment can document a vulnerability. Neither, by itself, demonstrates that the organization is becoming more resilient. Industrial risk isn't static. Asset conditions change, operational dependencies evolve, and an exposure that appeared manageable during a periodic assessment may become significantly more consequential. A recommendation without a named decision-maker and deadline is information, not control. Someone must have the authority to accept the exposure, fund the response or explain why another course is justified. Following the process is important, although it's not the same as preventing the loss. Insurance can help change the economics of prevention Insurers can make recommendations easier to act on by explaining the severity and urgency of an exposure, not simply recording that it exists. Brokers can connect risk-engineering findings with an organization's insurance and resilience priorities. Operators must determine whether to intervene or accept the exposure and take responsibility for the outcome. There is also a bigger opportunity here. Insurers and brokers possess extraordinary expertise in understanding, quantifying, and pricing risk. Much of that expertise has historically helped organizations prepare financially for potential losses. What if more of it could be applied to making prevention economically compelling before those losses occur? Imagine insurers, brokers, and industrial operators working from a more continuous, consequence-based understanding of emerging physical risk. Rather than relying primarily on historical losses and periodic assessments, they could better understand where exposure is developing, which conditions present the greatest business consequences, and where intervention could materially reduce risk. This wouldn't eliminate uncertainty or diminish the need for insurance. It could, however, create a stronger economic foundation for prevention and a more productive relationship between risk financing and operational decision-making. For decades, the insurance industry has helped businesses understand the financial consequences of what can go wrong. That expertise will remain indispensable, but the next opportunity is to help make the economics of what doesn't have to go wrong equally visible. We've become extraordinarily good at financing industrial failure. It's time to become just as disciplined about investing in its prevention. Andy Pruett

Now multiply that challenge across hundreds of assets and facilities, each presenting different levels of exposure. The question is no longer simply whether an individual intervention is justified. It's which interventions deserve priority when resources are limited, and the consequences extend across the enterprise. For decades, industry has developed sophisticated ways to measure losses after they occur. We need comparable discipline in understanding the economic value of preventing those losses before they happen. Capital should not only be deployed to absorb loss. It should be possible to direct it intelligently toward preventing loss. The standard for resilience must rise Risk assessments, inspections and engineering recommendations are essential. Completing those processes, however, doesn't necessarily mean an organization has addressed its most consequential exposures. An inspection can establish that a process was followed. A risk assessment can document a vulnerability. Neither, by itself, demonstrates that the organization is becoming more resilient. Industrial risk isn't static. Asset conditions change, operational dependencies evolve, and an exposure that appeared manageable during a periodic assessment may become significantly more consequential. A recommendation without a named decision-maker and deadline is information, not control. Someone must have the authority to accept the exposure, fund the response or explain why another course is justified. Following the process is important, although it's not the same as preventing the loss. Insurance can help change the economics of prevention Insurers can make recommendations easier to act on by explaining the severity and urgency of an exposure, not simply recording that it exists. Brokers can connect risk-engineering findings with an organization's insurance and resilience priorities. Operators must determine whether to intervene or accept the exposure and take responsibility for the outcome. There is also a bigger opportunity here. Insurers and brokers possess extraordinary expertise in understanding, quantifying, and pricing risk. Much of that expertise has historically helped organizations prepare financially for potential losses. What if more of it could be applied to making prevention economically compelling before those losses occur? Imagine insurers, brokers, and industrial operators working from a more continuous, consequence-based understanding of emerging physical risk. Rather than relying primarily on historical losses and periodic assessments, they could better understand where exposure is developing, which conditions present the greatest business consequences, and where intervention could materially reduce risk. This wouldn't eliminate uncertainty or diminish the need for insurance. It could, however, create a stronger economic foundation for prevention and a more productive relationship between risk financing and operational decision-making. For decades, the insurance industry has helped businesses understand the financial consequences of what can go wrong. That expertise will remain indispensable, but the next opportunity is to help make the economics of what doesn't have to go wrong equally visible. We've become extraordinarily good at financing industrial failure. It's time to become just as disciplined about investing in its prevention. items.summary: Why Can't We Fund Prevention? November 5, 2026 Image We've built an extraordinarily sophisticated financial system around industrial failure. We can price it, insure it, reserve capital for it, and finance recovery when it happens, but preventing that same failure often requires an entirely different standard of proof. Insurance covered approximately 42%, leaving nearly $60 billion to be absorbed elsewhere. Insurance's ability to fund recovery is indispensable. A proposal to prevent an asset failure faces a tougher test. Someone must prove the threat is serious, determine what intervention it warrants, and defend spending money on an event that might never happen. Failure has a funding mechanism. They receive risk-engineering reports, inspection findings, maintenance records and alerts from connected equipment. Yet information doesn't guarantee action. A temperature change, unusual vibration, or a deteriorating component has little meaning in isolation. Its significance depends on the asset's role in the operation. Is there redundancy? What production depends on it? What would a shutdown cost? Could a failure disrupt customers, supply chains or other facilities? Without that translation, recommendations can remain in reports while maintenance teams address more immediate demands and capital committees fund projects with clearer returns. A relatively minor condition on a critical asset may represent far greater exposure than a severe condition on equipment with sufficient redundancy. items.rss_description: High Street Insurance Partners said Tuesday it has acquired the retail brokerage business of Players Health, a Minneapolis-based specialty agency, and has launched a sports and fitness practice.
items.extracted_text: Terms of the deal were not disclosed. With the addition, Traverse City, Michigan-based High Street will provide specialty risk management services and insurance coverage to athletes, teams, leagues, facilities, fitness centers, event organizers and other sports-related organizations, the brokerage said in a statement. Players Health founder and CEO Tyrre Burks will lead High Street’s sports and fitness practice starting Dec. 1. Following the sale, Players Health, which is backed by Bluestone Equity Partners, will focus on expanding its sports and fitness managing general agent business, the company said in a separate statement. The agency said it plans to announce Mr. Burks’ successor following his departure. Willis Re Capital Solutions advised Players Health on the deal. High Street is the 21 st -largest broker of U.S. business according to Business Insurance’s latest ranking. items.extracted_text: Cat bond issuance hits $20bn at fastest pace in 2026, market size exceeds $66bn for first time - Artemis.bm Cat bond issuance hits $20bn at fastest pace in 2026, market size exceeds $66bn for first time - Artemis.bm Cat bond issuance hits $20bn at fastest pace in 2026, market size exceeds $66bn for first time 17th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans The catastrophe bond market has now surpassed $20 billion of issuance in 2026 across settled 144A catastrophe bonds and private cat bond deals tracked by Artemis so far, reaching the milestone one week ahead of last year’s pace. In addition, cat bond risk capital outstanding has exceeded $66 billion for the first time ever. With the catastrophe bond market pipeline continuing to build for the fourth-quarter, issuance remains on-track to near and perhaps even surpass the full-year record set in 2025. In 2025, the cat bond market reached $20 billion of settled issuance, across 144A cat bonds and private cat bonds we’d tracked, on November 25th. As our readers will be aware, 2025 went on to set a new full-year record. Find details in our quarterly market reports . With the settlement today of insurer SafePoint’s largest cat bond sponsorship in its history, the $650 million Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-2) deal, the market has now officially reached the $20 billion of issuance tracked by Artemis milestone at its quickest pace. Also of note, issuance of just Rule 144A catastrophe bonds will hit the $20 billion milestone tomorrow, with the settlement of VIG Re’s debut Charles Bridge Re 2026 DAC catastrophe bond. That 144A cat bond only $20 billion milestone was also reached on November 25th in 2025, so that record is going to be broken in 2026 as well. Even more notable in 2026, issuance of Rule 144A property catastrophe bonds only (so excluding any life, health or specialty lines deals) is now scheduled to reach the $20 billion milestone on November 23rd. That is a significantly quicker pace than 2025, when that pure property cat bond total was only reached on December 16th. All of which serves to underscore just how busy the catastrophe bond market and its participants have been this year, with the pace of cat bond issuance setting new records as the year continues. As things stand today on November 17th 2026, we’ve tracked over $20.37 billion of settled cat bond issuance , across 144A cat bonds and private deals. Analyse issuance in this interactive chart . The market pipeline currently contains targeted issuance of a further $3.286 billion of cat bond notes in the coming weeks as well, all scheduled to settle this year. Which means the latest projection we have for total issuance of 144A and private cat bonds once the current pipeline settles is for almost $23.66 billion. That’s still short of 2025’s record $25.6 billion, but with plenty of time left for the catastrophe bonds currently in the pipeline to upsize, or for more deals to be launched, a new annual issuance record remains possible in 2026. As of today, with the settlement of SafePoint’s latest and largest cat bond, Artemis’ measure for the outstanding catastrophe bond market, across 144A and the private cat bonds we’ve tracked, has exceeded $66 billion for the first time ever . Analyse the growth of the outstanding catastrophe bond market, by Artemis’ measure, in this interactive chart . That represents $4.69 billion, or almost 8% growth in catastrophe bond risk capital outstanding in 2026 so far. According to our data there are still $1.52 billion of cat bonds set to mature before the end of the year , so with the pipeline already showing $3.286 billion of cat bond notes expected to be issued at this time, additional growth in cat bond market size is expected before 2026 draws to a close. Whether the full-year issuance record gets broken in 2026 comes down to catastrophe bond deal-flow over the coming weeks. With sponsors recognising the clear and current opportunity to lock-in multi-year reinsurance protection from the capital markets at attractive rates, there is still every chance the full-year 2026 total gets very close to, or even exceeds 2025. items.extracted_text: P&C soft market deepens, but profitability cushion will gradually erode: Swiss Re - Artemis.bm P&C soft market deepens, but profitability cushion will gradually erode: Swiss Re - Artemis.bm P&C soft market deepens, but profitability cushion will gradually erode: Swiss Re 17th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Swiss Re has forecast this morning that global non-life insurance premium growth is expected to accelerate over the next couple of years. But competition is driving prices down even as risks become more complex and this is likely to continue, until the profitability cushion gets eroded over time, the reinsurer explained. Swiss Re’s Institute published a new sigma report today on the global outlook for the economy and insurance over the next two years. Global economic growth of 2.8% is forecast for 2027, an increase from an estimated 2.6% in 2026, followed by an expectation for 2.6% growth in 2028. For the global non-life insurance and reinsurance market, Swiss Re’s Institute forecasts accelerating premium growth, from a 0.5% base in 2026. For 2027, global non-life insurance premiums are forecast to grow by 1.0% in real terms, while for 2028 that is expected to double to 2.0% growth. However, as the global non-life P&C insurance and reinsurance market continues to soften, Swiss Re expects that non-life premium growth will shift from being pricing-led, to being exposure-led going forwards. “Growth will increasingly come from more assets and businesses needing insurance rather than higher prices,” the reinsurer explained today. As a result, non-life insurer return-on-equity (ROE) is expected to dwindle due to reduced underwriting margins. Swiss Re’s Institute saw non-life insurer ROE’s at 12.7% in 2026, but set to decline to 10.3% in 2027, after which the reinsurance firm believes ROE’s will continue to decline towards their cost-of-capital, at approximately 7.3% over the medium term. Rising risks and new types or classes of risk are driving demand for protection, Swiss Re explains. But, the market has been a victim of its own profitability success in recent years and it is the weight of capital, largely from profits, that is weighing on non-life re/insurance pricing now. Jason Richards, CEO P&C Reinsurance UK & Ireland at Swiss Re, commented, “The insurance industry is well capitalised, putting it in a strong position to provide protection in an increasingly complex risk landscape. But having capital available is not the same as underwriting every risk. As risks become more interconnected, understanding how they accumulate is key to the industry deploying capacity where it can make the greatest difference and providing sustainable protection.” The Swiss Re Institute sigma report states, “High non-life profitability driven among other factors, by strong investment income, is prolonging the soft market. But this support should fade as lower prices earn through portfolios and return on equity (RoE) converges towards the cost of capital. “As excess returns narrow and risks become more interconnected, insurers may become more selective in deploying capacity, despite abundant capital. This distinction between capital and capacity matters more as natural catastrophe, liability and other risks become more complex and correlated, leading to greater differentiation in pricing and growth across risk pools.” The non-life insurance and reinsurance industry currently has a capital cushion, created by its recent historical profitability, which is exacerbating the softening marketplace. As returns converge towards the cost-of-capital, Swiss Re believes the softening may normalise at a certain level. Swiss Re’s Institute believes the convergence of three factors could help to limit how low pricing can go in non-life insurance markets. First, the fact premium growth is becoming exposure led, while in non-life AI-related capex and emerging markets are expanding the pool of insurable assets. Second, the market is expected to become increasingly fragmented and selective across performance of policies and portfolios, as well as risk understanding. And third, the increasing complexity and interconnectedness of risks. “These pressures could limit how far pricing and terms can soften, even in a market with abundant capital,” the sigma report states. As the softening continues Swiss Re expects, “Industry-wide underwriting margins to slide from 4.4% of premiums earned in 2026 to 1.7% in 2027, and to barely above 0% in 2028.” Which would be, “Roughly in line with the 2016‒2022 average during the last global soft cycle.” But the cushion of profitability is expected to erode over time, which may help to reduce some of the pressure, Swiss Re believes. “This cushion may not last much longer as softer prices earn through portfolios, reserve support weakens and catastrophe losses revert towards trend. At the same time, claims severity pressures will persist given a volatile risk backdrop. Inflation in insurance-relevant categories, such as construction costs and medical treatment, is running above headline CPI inflation. The soft market may persist in the near term but underwriting conditions should gradually stabilise as industry RoE slides towards the cost of capital,” the reinsurer’s Institute explains in the sigma report. Finally, Swiss Re also highlights that capital destruction is not always required for a soft market to come to an end. Rising uncertainty around the risks themselves can also be a trigger for a repricing. At the same time, the increasing complexity of risks and their interconnected nature can also be a catalyst for more pressure on sector capacity, something illustrated by the global capital expenditure around artificial intelligence, technology and energy. But ultimately, it is that capital cushion which has been created through hard market pricing years where profits have been sky-high that is the cause of the greatest pressure, as seen in reinsurance and even in areas such as catastrophe bonds where coupon earnings have been boosting the insurance-linked securities capital base. The only question is how long it takes to erode the profitability cushion this time around? We have seen it take year’s in previous cycles. It seems likely that some kind of exogenous shock(s) from outside the industry combined with elevated catastrophe loss experience, may now be required for any kind of meaningful repricing to occur. items.title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.original_title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.rss_title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.rss_description: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop' PaulCarroll Tue, 11/10/2026 - 12:55 The notion that there must always be a "human in the loop" has become de rigueur in any discussion of AI implementation in business. The cynical side of me suspects that part of the reason is to reassure everyone that AI won't lead to mass layoffs, but there are also plenty of practical reasons to have humans check the work of AIs. Or maybe not. At least not for long. A recent article in Harvard Business Review argues that human supervisors quickly become numb and simply approve the recommendations of the AI as it becomes increasingly accurate. And I think the author has a point, based on what I've seen of human/AI interactions in semi-autonomous cars. There needs to be a better way. Let's have a look. Early in the development of its driverless cars, Google gave demo models to employees. Google warned them that the AI wasn't perfect and instructed them to have their hands on the wheel, always ready to take control. That worked... for a little while. A very little while. As the AI proved to be reliable, the drivers began to relax their hold on the wheel, then started to take their eyes off the road, then began reading or looking at their phones. When the car signaled that the drivers had to take over, they needed perhaps 10 seconds to fully reengage. Given that a car going 60mph travels nearly 300 yards in 10 seconds, Google realized its hybrid approach wouldn't work and committed to producing only cars that could be fully autonomous. Other makers of autonomous vehicles, most notably Tesla, continue to offer cars that take a hybrid, human/AI approach, but I think that's irresponsible (as I wrote at length a year ago). Now, an article in Harvard Business Review offers a similar view about the dangers of having a "human in the loop" to supervise work done by AIs. The author, a senior fellow at Cal, writes: "Decades of research on automation show that better automation systems lead to worse human safety layers; as automation grows more reliable, the people monitoring it grow complacent, their skills atrophy, and they become less attentive.... AI compounds the problem. Its failures sound as confident, fluent, and well-structured as its successes.... "Even when validation works and people catch errors, every correction is captured as training data. Each exception a person handles teaches the system to handle that exception; the better the data, the smaller the scope of human validation needed in the future." The article says the lack of reliability of the humans in the loop is actually just the start of the problem. He writes: "The larger problem with the human-in-the-loop organization, though, is that the entire blueprint reads the transformation backwards. It organizes the company around the shrinking frontier of what machines can’t yet do. But there’s a larger opportunity here. Because AI removes constraints, it enables new combinations of work, new decision rights, and new forms of value. Organizations, accordingly, have an opportunity to reorganize and 'rebundle' around those new decisions rather than the shrinking residue of the old work." He goes on to lay out how to think about rebundling: "Instead of asking which tasks the machine can take over, leading organizations should ask which new roles the technology makes possible, and then redesign the organization around them." He lists several steps that can lead you to new approaches, which seem intriguing and which you may want to explore. For now, though, I just want to make the point that "human in the loop" isn't a panacea, certainly not in the long term. The reviewers of AI work can quickly become as reliant on the AI as those Google employees who found themselves with their hands off the wheel, their eyes off the road and their minds far away from driving when a problem popped up in front of them. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll An HBR article argues that human supervisors quickly become unreliable as the AI becomes increasingly accurate. items.extracted_text: AI Advances Coincide With Sharp Rise in Cyber Incidents, Marsh Data Shows Article 0 Comments Artificial intelligence is accelerating the pace and scale of cyberattacks, leading to more incidents reported by businesses and creating new challenges for companies and their insurers, data from insurance broker Marsh showed. “The signs that the attackers are using AI enabled and agentic tools to identify vulnerabilities is happening. So I would say we could attribute AI to a significant number of these,” Meredith Schnur, Marsh Risk’s US and Canada cyber practice leader, told Reuters in an interview this week. Marsh said its clients reported 105 cyber incidents in the last two weeks of October, more than double the 48 recorded in the final two weeks of May. Schnur said the speed and scale of AI tool adoption, coupled with organizations taking longer to contain attacks and respond to incidents, were the main factors driving the recent increase in cyber incident volumes. “AI is not a peril, its an amplification of risk in all areas,” Schnur said AI is enabling attackers to identify and exploit longstanding vulnerabilities, including unpatched software, exposed systems and weak identity controls, at a much faster pace. As AI tools become more widely accessible, attackers can scale their operations with fewer resources, widening the pool of potential targets and putting pressure on businesses. According to GlobalData, cyber insurance premiums are set to grow at a faster pace over the next two years as businesses respond to rising attack frequency. It expects global cyber insurance premiums to rise 6.9% to $16.6 billion in 2026, before accelerating to 10% growth in 2027 to reach $18.3 billion. items.extracted_text: L’Oreal US Settles Hair Relaxer Cancer Cases During First Trial Article 0 Comments Four women who said they were diagnosed with cancer as a result of chemical hair straightening products reached a settlement on Monday with L’Oreal’s U.S. subsidiary and other companies during a trial in Chicago, according to their attorneys. The women are among thousands who have sued the companies, alleging that years of using chemical hair straighteners caused them to develop gynecologic cancers. The cases, which were the first to go to trial, settled for a confidential sum, the lawyers said. A spokesperson for L’Oreal said the company’s highest priority is the health and wellbeing of its consumers, and it remains confident in the safety of its SoftSheen-Carson brand hair products, which include hair relaxers. “L’Oréal USA strictly follows all regulations in every market in which it operates, and its products are always subject to a rigorous scientific evaluation of their safety,” the spokesperson said. In a statement, Danielle Ward Mason, an attorney for the women, MaryAnne Lindsey, Surenthia Jenkins, Miranda Lofton and Sandra Simpson, said she hoped the settlement would give the women a sense of justice. The women sued L’Oreal’s U.S. subsidiary and several other makers of the products in Cook County, Illinois, in 2023 and 2024. The trial began on November 9 with jury selection. While some cases have been filed in state court, more than 12,700 cases over the claims are centralized before a judge in federal court in Chicago, court records show. The products, which have been marketed under the names Dark and Lovely, Optimum and other brands, promise to permanently straighten textured hair and have been widely marketed to Black women. The first lawsuits hit the docket after the 2022 release of a study done ⁠by the National Institutes of Health that found women who used the products several times a year were more than twice as likely to develop uterine cancer. L’Oreal has said the study did not establish a causal link between the ⁠use of the products and any conditions alleged by the plaintiffs. At least two states, Arizona and Minnesota, sued L’Oreal over the products this year, alleging that the company had misled women about their safety. items.extracted_text: NHTSA Opens Probe into 1 Million Hondas Over Auto Stop-Start Failures Article 0 Comments The U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said on Monday it had opened an engineering analysis into 1,033,632 Honda vehicles in the country over concerns that their engines failed to restart after being shut off by the vehicles’ automatic stop-start system. The agency said it has received 701 complaints about the auto stop-start feature in the 2024-2026 model year Honda Odyssey, Passport, Ridgeline and Pilot, as well as the Acura MDX. The auto stop-start system is designed to save fuel. It turns off the engine when the vehicle comes to a complete stop and is supposed to restart it when the driver takes their foot off the brake. Related: Honda Recalling 600,000 US Vehicles Over Steering Assist Software However, drivers have complained that their engines did not restart after being shut off by the system. NHTSA is already looking into similar stop-start problems in some Honda vehicles under a separate investigation. That probe covers all the vehicles in the new review except the 2026 models. The regulator said that while both groups of vehicles show similar failures, the vehicles in the new investigation appear to have different root causes and respond differently to repairs. The new probe comes a week after Honda recalled 635,808 vehicles in the U.S. over a software glitch that could switch off power steering assist, making them harder to steer. items.title: Compass Sues Multiple Listing Services, Upping Antitrust Row
items.original_title: Compass Sues Multiple Listing Services, Upping Antitrust Row
items.rss_title: Compass Sues Multiple Listing Services, Upping Antitrust Row
items.rss_description: A feud over how consumers can buy and sell homes escalated on Thursday with a slew of antitrust lawsuits filed across the country by the top U.S. broker for residential properties. In more than a dozen lawsuits filed in federal …
items.extracted_text: Compass Sues Multiple Listing Services, Upping Antitrust Row Article 0 Comments A feud over how consumers can buy and sell homes escalated on Thursday with a slew of antitrust lawsuits filed across the country by the top U.S. broker for residential properties. In more than a dozen lawsuits filed in federal courts, Compass Inc. accused 15 listing services across eight states of adopting anticompetitive rules over access to data on homes being put up for sale. The company sued MLS networks that require listings be submitted to the shared database within one business day or the agent can face fines, suspension or expulsion from the service. Supporters of these rules say they help ensure every agent has equal access to listings on the platforms that have become the industry standard. The legal battle pits Compass’ effort to take control over home listings data against the decades-old industry practice of relying on multiple listing services across the country, which aggregate listings for a particular geographic area and were previously only available to real estate agents who were members of the National Association of Realtors. Compass’s 15 suits target six services in California, including those covering San Diego and the East Bay of San Francisco three services in North Carolina the largest multiple listing service in New York covering homes for sale in New York City and Long Island the listings service for the greater Houston region in Texas as well as the largest listings databases in Arizona, Colorado, Florida and Minnesota. None of the 15 listing services immediately responded to requests for comment on the suits. In a statement, Compass said it believes that homeowners and their agents should make decisions about how to market homes for sale and said that seven of the top 25 listing services allow public marketing of exclusives. In 2025, the National Association of Realtors loosened it’s “clear-cooperation” policies, which required brokers to submit home listings to the MLS within one day of publicly marketing a property. That change allowed the 400-plus public databases to formulate standards for when a seller wants to delay marketing a listing widely. The rule was originally implemented to limit private listings that critics say harm buyers while making it more difficult for sellers to maximize profits. In a statement Friday, NAR said that multiple listing services provide consumers with broader market exposure, reliable property data and equal access to available properties, and that each real estate agent agrees to abide by the services’ terms when they join. The pullback on clear cooperation policies paved the way for Compass – a player in major markets including New York, Chicago and San Francisco – to adopt a strategy of initially holding back some home listings from the MLS databases that had become the industry standard in an effort to amass a listings network they control. Compass employs a three-phased marketing strategy where it delays making home listings publicly available by first marketing homes internally to its own brokers before moving to a “coming soon” designation where they appear only on the Compass website. The company maintains that strategy results in higher sales prices and more options for home sellers. Rival brokerages disagree. It’s why some competitors, including four of the country’s largest brokerages — AGNT, HomeServices of America, Keller Williams and Real REMAX Group — are teaming up on a national residential real estate data-sharing initiative called Open Real Estate, allowing participants to share home listings on a platform that will start in 2027. Bess Freedman, the chief executive officer of brokerage Brown Harris Stevens and a participating member of Open Real Estate, said Compass appears to be using strong-arm tactics to control more information and data distribution when it already has enormous market share across the country. “Compass is clearly not speaking on behalf of the industry nor consumers with these lawsuits,” Freedman said. “The industry is already reeling from high interest rates, high prices, and low inventory, and suing MLSs in an effort to keep more listings hidden is a disservice to the overall brokerage community, buyers and sellers, and fair housing principles.” Seven of the multiple listing services sued Compass in New York federal court last month seeking a court order in support of their listings rules. The seven services said they require brokers who want access to their databases to agree to provide their own listings publicly, but also offer options for more limited marketing. OneKey, the New York database, separately sued Compass along with the California Regional Multiple Listing Service over the same issue. Compass subsequently filed its own antitrust case against CRMLS, the largest MLS in California which covers 22 counties in the state, including areas around Los Angeles, the San Francisco Bay Area and San Diego. Both lawsuits remain pending. Top photo: A Compass office in San Francisco, California, on Monday, April 29, 2024. Compass Inc. is scheduled to release earnings figures on May 8. Bloomberg. items.title: Commercial insurance premiums fall 1.3% in third quarter: CIAB
items.original_title: Commercial insurance premiums fall 1.3% in third quarter: CIAB
items.rss_title: Commercial insurance premiums fall 1.3% in third quarter: CIAB
items.rss_description: Commercial insurance premiums fell 1.3% on average in the third quarter, marking the third consecutive quarterly decline, according to the Council of Insurance Agents & Brokers’ latest survey.
items.extracted_text: While the decrease was smaller than the 2% decline reported in the second quarter, increased competition among insurers continued to put downward pressure on prices, the Council said. Pricing varied significantly by line, with commercial property insurance premiums decreasing the most, down 6.2%, followed by directors and officers liability, down 4.1%, and workers compensation, down 3.6%. Premiums in other major lines continued to rise, with commercial auto up 6.7%, general liability up 3.1% and umbrella liability up 2.8%. Commercial auto premiums have increased each quarter for more than 15 years, with the third-quarter rise accelerating from 4.5% in the second quarter. Umbrella liability premium increases moderated from 5.3% in the second quarter. In other lines, business interruption premiums fell 2.2%, terrorism declined 2.1%, construction decreased 1.7% and cyber liability edged down 0.2%, according to the survey. By account size, average premiums fell 3.1% for large accounts, 0.7% for medium accounts and 0.2% for small accounts. items.extracted_text: The Hartford seeks lower pricing for $280m Foundation Re IV 2027-1 cat bond - Artemis.bm The Hartford seeks lower pricing for $280m Foundation Re IV 2027-1 cat bond - Artemis.bm The Hartford seeks lower pricing for $280m Foundation Re IV 2027-1 cat bond 17th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans The Hartford continues to target $280 million of multi-peril collateralized reinsurance protection from its new Foundation Re IV Ltd. (Series 2027-1) catastrophe bond, but like other recent deals the spread guidance has fallen as the insurer seeks lower pricing, Artemis understands. US primary property and casualty insurer The Hartford returned to the catastrophe bond market at the end of October, looking to secure $280 million or more in multi-peril collateralized catastrophe reinsurance protection from the capital markets through its eighth cat bond sponsorship. As we said at the time, The Hartford has $200 million of multi-peril catastrophe reinsurance from its Foundation Re IV 2023-1 issuance that matures around the end of 2026, so this new deal appears a renewal of sorts for that expiring capital markets backed reinsurance protection. We’ve now learned that The Hartford remains on-track with its new cat bond, still targeting the same $280 million of protection, but with the price guidance now revised at a lower level as the insurer targets strong execution in the market. As a result, we understand Foundation Re IV Ltd. is still offering investors a $280 million single tranche of Series 2027-1 Class A notes, that will provide The Hartford fully-collateralized US named storm and earthquake protection across a four calendar year term running to the end of 2030, on an indemnity trigger and per-occurrence basis. The $280 million of Foundation Re IV Ltd. Series 2027-1 Class A notes have an initial base expected loss of 1.56% and were first offered to cat bond investors with spread price guidance in a range from 3% to 3.5%. We’re now told that the notes price guidance range has been revised and lowered to between 2.75% and 3%, indicating ample demand from investors and potentially strong execution for the sponsoring insurer. items.extracted_text: Reports Show Insurance Loss Estimates for Microsoft Outage Range From $100M to $700M Article 0 Comments Global cyber insured losses from the Microsoft 365 outage on Nov. 12-14 are estimated by various industry observers to range from $100 million to $700 million. CyberCube, the cyber risk analytics provider, estimates that the outage will most likely be less than $100 million, with a conservative upper limit estimated at $350 million. Read more: Hours-Long Microsoft Outage Disrupts Businesses, Governments Globally Credit ratings agency Morningstar DBRS said: “In our view, the overall credit impact of the Microsoft outage on insurers is likely to be limited, with global insured losses estimates at US$300 million to US$500 million….” Insurance broker Acrisure had a higher insurance loss estimate of US$700 million. “Overall, the impact on the insurance market is expected to be minimal, with most losses likely limited to short-term productivity and operational delays,” said Marsh Re in a report titled “ Delivery failed: Microsoft 365 outage .” “Claims may nevertheless arise where policyholders relied on Microsoft 365 for critical, time-sensitive, or revenue-generating activities and the applicable waiting period was exceeded,” Marsh Re added. “The event also highlights the systemic and accumulation risks associated with reliance on a dominant technology provider, even where individual claims remain limited.” Technical Issue, Not Cyber Activity Microsoft attributed the outage to a technical issue introduced during a network capacity upgrade, not cyber activity, CyberCube said, explaining that severe disruption lasted about 18 hours, and the event ran roughly 38 hours in total – well beyond the eight to 12 hour waiting periods common in contingent system failure cover. Despite the duration of the outage, CyberCube expects several factors will suppress insured losses. “Cover only responds where policies extend business interruption to non-malicious system failure at an outside provider. Impacts reported from the event all focus on the inconvenience and productivity loss, with workarounds widely available and little to no mention of lost revenue,” the company said. “Simply put, email is not in the critical transaction path of most businesses.” As of Nov. 13, Marsh Re described the outage as “a significant but uneven disruption with broad geographic exposure and progressive recovery,” but not a complete Microsoft 365 outage, a cloud infrastructure failure, nor or a cyberattack. “Given that the disruption has exceeded 12 hours, potential business interruption or contingent business interruption losses may be relevant where insureds relied on Microsoft 365 for critical, time-sensitive, or revenue-generating operations,” Marsh Re said. “Overall, however, the impact on the insurance market is expected to be minimal, given the uneven nature of the disruption and likelihood that most losses will be limited to short-term productivity and operational delays.” Read more: Microsoft Says Services Fully Restored After Outage Roiled World “This event once again reminds us how the technology world is concentrated in the hands of a few key providers. But it also reminds us that not all layers of the technology stack are equally critical to business operations,” commented Jon Laux, CyberCube’s vice president of Products and Analytics. “Factors that informed our loss estimates include the relatively short duration of this event, the absence of any reported data corruption or leakage, and the ease with which companies fell back on alternative communication channels to email,” he said. “The Microsoft outage could result in a number of insurance claims, mostly related to businesses experiencing financial losses, operational disruptions, and delays in serving customers,” according to Mario de Cicco, vice president, European Financial Institutions, Morningstar DBRS. “However, not all businesses will automatically be entitled to compensation, as this depends on the terms and conditions of their insurance policies,” di Cicco added. “Some cyber insurance policies only cover losses caused by malicious cyberattacks, whereas the Microsoft outage appears to have resulted from a technical failure rather than a deliberate attack. Additionally, some policies include waiting periods before business interruption cover becomes effective.” As a useful comparison, di Cicco discussed the 2024 CrowdStrike outage. “The issue was caused by a faulty software update that affected around 8.5 million Windows devices worldwide. It disrupted major industries, including airlines, hospitals, banks, and retailers, and caused flight cancellations, business interruptions, financial losses, and delays in services that generated insurance claims,” he said. The CrowdStrike had a significant global impact, generating insurance losses between US$400 million and US$1.5 billion, he said, quoting CyberCube estimates. On the other hand, the Microsoft outage is estimated to cost insurers US$300 million to US$500 million, well below the CrowdStrike outage estimates, he added. “Both outages highlight the credit and operational risks that insurance companies face from their growing reliance on concentrated technology providers and server infrastructures, the consequences of which are difficult to predict,” di Cicco said. “The ultimate impact on claims will be determined by the scope of policy coverage, and insurers’ responses will depend on the waiting period, deductibles, sublimits, and exclusions. Economic losses outside of policy terms and conditions will be borne by businesses.” The report from Marsh Re explained that large technology-service incidents, including notable Google-related disruptions and the CrowdStrike outage, “demonstrate that widely used technology can create global exposure.” “From an accumulation perspective, Microsoft’s market dominance highlights the potential for a cyber systemic event to arise from disruption to this single point of failure risk,” Marsh Re said. “However, significant technology incidents do not necessarily translate into meaningful losses across the insurance market. Loss outcomes depend on the duration, severity, and type of impairment experienced by each insured,” Marsh Re added. (See chart below). Source: Marsh Re A report published by Acrisure London Wholesale detailed how business interruption works within cyber policies. “Cyber policies typically include coverage for business interruption as a result of system failure. Where the failure occurs at an external provider, dependent or contingent business interruption cover may respond,” Acrisure said in the report titled “The Cyber Insurance Implications of Microsoft’s Outage.” “However, the scope varies as some policies are triggered by any external provider while others restrict cover to non-IT providers or even a scheduled list of suppliers. Establishing whether Microsoft and the affected services fall within those definitions is therefore essential,” said the report, which was authored by Lara Wheeler , assistant vice president with Acrisure London Wholesale’s Cyber team. The report explained that business Interruption is also generally subject to a time retention, known as a “waiting period,” which is typically 8-12 hours. “The duration of the Microsoft outage means many businesses will have already exceeded their applicable waiting period. However, businesses will still need to demonstrate and quantify financial loss directly resulting from the interruption to establish coverage,” the Acrisure report continued. Top photo: A Microsoft logo and sign outside the Microsoft Visitor Center are seen at the company’s headquarters on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, in Redmond, Wash. (AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson, File). items.extracted_text: NormanMax parametric Syndicate 3939 more than doubles GWP, gets $65m capacity approved for 2027 - Artemis.bm NormanMax parametric Syndicate 3939 more than doubles GWP, gets $65m capacity approved for 2027 - Artemis.bm NormanMax parametric Syndicate 3939 more than doubles GWP, gets $65m capacity approved for 2027 17th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans NormanMax Syndicate 3939, the first pure parametric global syndicate in the Lloyd’s marketplace, has reported a more than doubling of gross premiums written in 2026 at an 87.3% combined ratio and has obtained approval for an increase to $65 million of capacity in 2027. NormanMax Insurance Holdings, the US based parametric insurance and reinsurance group, launched its dedicated parametric syndicate 3939 at Lloyd’s in 2024 and began underwriting in May that year . In 2026, NormanMax Syndicate 3939 is now completing its third year of account in the Lloyd’s market and has reported $3.2 million in profits for the first nine months of 2026. For the first nine months to September 30th 2026, the parametric syndicate underwrote $53.8 million of gross written premium, more than doubling the $23.8 million written in full-year 2025. By November 10th, the 2026 Year of Account had already written $46.7 million against its $50 million of capacity that was approved. Within this, NormanMax Syndicate 3939 has expanded its footprint, bringing new sources of parametric risk into the Lloyd’s marketplace, as the company noted that non-cat weather is now a significant contributor to its portfolio. The non-cat weather business consists of short-tail underwriting business with low acquisition costs, which is a positive diversifier to the natural catastrophe focused book. NormanMax Syndicate’s Weather Transformer portfolio of business now spans the United States, Europe and Australia, and the company has also recently added its first transaction in Japan. Lloyd’s has now approved the NormanMax Syndicate for increased capacity of $65 million for 2027, as it continues to target expansion. For 2027, a key priority for the company is to add consortium capacity alongside the Syndicate, which NormanMax expects will deliver additional fees to help reduce expenses and boost its net income. Bradley I. Meier, Chairman, President and CEO of NormanMax Insurance Holdings and CEO of Syndicate 3939, commented, “On behalf of the Board and management team, thank you to the members of S3939 for their continued support, and to Apollo, Lloyd’s, our brokers and business partners for their confidence in the platform. “We thank Apollo in particular for their efforts in securing approval of our 2027 plan. We look forward to reporting a strong start to 2027.” For the first nine months of calendar year 2026, NormanMax parametric Syndicate 3939 delivered a GAAP profit of $3.2 million, against a combined ratio of 87.3% and a brokerage ratio of 18%, the company reported. While the third-quarter of the year saw events bringing claims against its Weather Transformer business, NormanMax noted that all of these have already been paid. In addition, $1.3 million of claims were caused by Hurricane Isaias and these are currently being settled. NormanMax highlighted the speed of claims settlement, one of the key features and deliverables of its parametric insurance and reinsurance products. Looking back to the prior year of account, NormanMax reported that 2025 is now forecast to close with an ultimate profit of $1.5 million, an improvement from the $3 million ultimate loss forecast at the end of the calendar year. At this stage, the 2026 Year of Account is forecast at a small ultimate loss of $0.8 million, which the company explained reflects prudent reserving on Weather Transformer business. Demonstrating efficiency improvements and growing platform scale, NormanMax Syndicate 3939 has seen its year of account expense ratio fall to 12.6% in 2026, from 29% for 2025. Looking ahead, NormanMax said that from the start of 2027 it expects the year of account calendar-year and year-of-account premium will be more closely aligned, making its results easier to follow. In addition, renewals of the delegated binders, including NMIS and FloodFlash, and of its Weather Transformer quota share reinsurance arrangement are being prepared for early January. With now two and half years of operation behind it, the parametric specialist Lloyd’s syndicate is demonstrating the differentiation this brings to the market, complementing traditional insurance and creating new opportunities for brokers, cedents and capital providers. items.title: Viewpoint: When AI Leaves the Screen, the Stakes Change
items.original_title: Viewpoint: When AI Leaves the Screen, the Stakes Change
items.rss_title: Viewpoint: When AI Leaves the Screen, the Stakes Change

items.extracted_text: Viewpoint: When AI Leaves the Screen, the Stakes Change Article 0 Comments On Nov. 13, routine work on the Federal Aviation Administration’s telecommunications network appears to have helped bring American air travel to a halt. Preliminary findings point to two sites: a remote radio site in Arkansas, where a contractor had deployed a new router, and a radar site in Texas. The root cause remains under investigation. A flood of connection attempts destabilized the agency’s legacy equipment, and the FAA grounded departures nationwide. Every aircraft landed safely. But a digital failure had stopped physical operations across an entire country. Microsoft and Workday suffered major outages the same week. Officials at the FAA and Microsoft have said artificial intelligence played no role, and nothing reported links Workday’s outage to AI. Notably, the FAA had expanded a new AI system for flight planning and traffic management nationwide just three days before the ground stop officials ruled it out as a cause. Together, though, these incidents show how routine maintenance, upgrades and testing can ripple through interconnected systems in ways their operators never anticipated. Now consider what happens when the technology being introduced can make its own decisions, initiate its own actions and move physical machinery. This is the emerging world of physical AI. AI Is Leaving The Screen For most people, AI still lives on a screen. It drafts documents, answers questions and recommends decisions. When it fails, the consequences are usually financial, contractual or reputational. That is changing quickly. Autonomous vehicles navigate public roads. Robots handle materials, operate manufacturing equipment and share warehouses with people. Intelligent systems regulate buildings’ electrical and mechanical infrastructure. Agricultural machinery works without continuous human direction. Each combines AI with sensors, mechanical equipment and physical environments that were often designed long before autonomous decision-making was practical. The potential benefits are substantial. So are the risks, because a physical AI failure can damage property, halt production or injure people in seconds. A Failure at The Intersection The October 2023 incident involving a Cruise robotaxi in San Francisco shows what these failures look like. A pedestrian struck by a hit-and-run driver was thrown into the robotaxi’s path. The vehicle braked and stopped, then attempted to pull over, dragging her about 20 feet because its systems did not detect that she was underneath. The failure did not sit neatly inside the AI. It arose where the software, its sensors, another driver’s actions and an unanticipated situation met. What followed was just as instructive. Cruise’s initial reports to federal regulators omitted the dragging, which the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration identified after reviewing video it had requested. The company agreed to pay a $1.5 million NHTSA penalty and later a $500,000 criminal fine under a deferred prosecution agreement in which it admitted submitting a false report to influence a federal investigation. In physical AI, what the machine recorded, and how the company handled that record, can matter as much as what the machine did. One Incident, Several Investigations A significant physical AI incident cannot be understood through a single discipline. Several investigations must proceed together. Forensic engineers determine whether sensors, mechanical components, software, electrical systems or safety controls contributed. Human factors specialists examine how people interacted with the autonomous equipment, whether warnings were adequate and whether there was a reasonable opportunity to intervene. Digital investigators reconstruct what the machine perceived, what it decided and what commands it issued. That depends on preserving sensor readings, model versions, operating logs and telemetry before they are overwritten, sometimes within hours. Financial experts then measure the losses: property damage, business interruption, lost profits, remediation costs and, in some cases, lasting impairment of valuable business assets. Attorneys and insurers face the questions that follow. Was the failure foreseeable? Did it stem from a defective product, poor integration, improper maintenance or unreasonable reliance on automation? Who bears responsibility, and which policies respond? None of these can be answered without the technical record. Physical AI is creating a new category of disputes that cuts across conventional professional boundaries. For insurers, the coverage questions may be the least settled of all. When a compromised or malfunctioning control system causes bodily injury or property damage, the loss can fall between cyber and general liability programs, and which one responds is often genuinely unsettled. An autonomous machine also raises questions conventional adjusting protocols do not answer: Can it be repaired? Must the model be retrained, at what cost and by whom? If the model itself was corrupted, is that a physical loss or a cyber loss? The Business Case Must Include The Downside In decades of valuing intellectual property and other intangible assets, I have seen that technology creates value only when it can be successfully deployed and sustained. The benefits of innovation must be weighed against the risks of putting it to work. A manufacturer might justify a multimillion-dollar investment in autonomous equipment on labor savings and higher throughput. But a single preventable integration failure that causes injury or an extended shutdown could erase years of those savings. Even with insurance, the company may still absorb deductibles, uncovered losses, litigation, regulatory scrutiny and damaged customer relationships. The business case for physical AI cannot end with whether the technology works. It must also show that the organization can operate it safely, contain failures, preserve evidence and respond when something goes wrong. That means testing interconnected systems together, setting clear limits on autonomous authority, maintaining effective human oversight, documenting every change to models and equipment, and rehearsing incident response before it is needed. Three Questions Before Approving Capital — Or Binding Coverage Responsible risk management should not become an excuse to delay innovation. Moving quickly and understanding downside exposure are not mutually exclusive. Before approving capital for physical AI, management and boards should require answers to three questions: If something goes wrong, can we reconstruct what happened, establish responsibility and measure the loss? Are our existing infrastructure, people and safety controls prepared for what these systems can do? Does our business case account for the cost of a failure, and not only the savings when everything works? Brokers and underwriters should ask a parallel set before binding coverage: How was the system validated, and within what operating limits? Who can override it? Are incident logs retained? How are model updates and equipment changes controlled? The organizations that answer those questions honestly will be the ones that capture the value of physical AI rather than litigate it.
